three-sisters-agriculture.name: Three Sisters
three-sisters-agriculture.summary: A companion-planting method combining maize, beans and squash, in which each crop supports the others, developed by Indigenous peoples of the Americas.

ta-no.name: Taíno
ta-no.summary: Indigenous people of the West Indies, part of the Arawak group, who lived in agricultural societies led by caciques and were the first New World peoples encountered by non-Norse Europeans.

ancestral-puebloans.name: Ancestral Puebloans
ancestral-puebloans.summary: An ancient Native American culture spanning the Four Corners region of the US, living in pit houses, clan structures and cliff dwellings, linked by a network of communities across the Colorado Plateau.

l-anse-aux-meadows.name: L'Anse aux Meadows
l-anse-aux-meadows.summary: A Norse settlement site on Newfoundland's northern tip, dated to around 1000 CE by carbon and tree-ring evidence, the only confirmed pre-Columbian European site in the Americas outside Greenland.

navajo.name: Navajo
navajo.summary: An Indigenous people of the southwestern United States, known to themselves as Diné, with the largest populations in Arizona and New Mexico and a reservation spanning the Four Corners region.

apache.name: Apache
apache.summary: Several related Southern Athabaskan-speaking peoples of the Southwest and southern Plains who migrated there between 1000 and 1500 CE and later fought Spanish, Mexican and U.S. forces.

ute-people.name: Ute people
ute-people.summary: An Indigenous people of the Great Basin and Colorado Plateau, in present-day Utah, Colorado and New Mexico, who kept a hunter-gatherer way of life.

nixtamalization.name: Nixtamalization
nixtamalization.summary: A process of soaking and cooking maize in an alkaline solution such as limewater, which improves its nutrition and flavor and makes it possible to form dough (masa).

blackfoot-confederacy.name: Blackfoot Confederacy
blackfoot-confederacy.summary: An alliance of related Indigenous peoples of the northern Great Plains in the US and Canada, once nomadic bison hunters who used horses and firearms from the 1700s to expand their territory.

cheyenne.name: Cheyenne
cheyenne.summary: An Indigenous Great Plains people who moved from Great Lakes woodlands to the Northern Plains and adopted horse culture by the early 18th century.

southeastern-ceremonial-complex.name: Southeastern Ceremonial Complex
southeastern-ceremonial-complex.summary: Modern scholars' name for the shared artistic styles, iconography and ceremonies of the Mississippian culture from 1200 to 1650 CE, once mistakenly thought linked to Mesoamerica.

wulfing-cache.name: Wulfing cache
wulfing-cache.summary: Set of eight Mississippian copper plates found in Missouri in 1906, whose repoussé designs helped archaeologists define the Southeastern Ceremonial Complex.

pueblo-bonito.name: Pueblo Bonito
pueblo-bonito.summary: The largest and best-known great house in Chaco Canyon, New Mexico, built and occupied by Ancestral Puebloans between about 828 and 1126, called an archaeological icon on par with Stonehenge or Machu Picchu.

chaco-culture-national-historical-park.name: Chaco Canyon
chaco-culture-national-historical-park.summary: A remote New Mexico canyon that was a major Ancestral Puebloan cultural center from 900 to 1150, where large stone complexes were built before drought led to abandonment.

cahokia-woodhenge.name: Cahokia Woodhenge
cahokia-woodhenge.summary: A series of large timber circles near Cahokia's Monks Mound, built between 900 and 1100 CE and used to track solstice and equinox sunrises.

cahokia.name: Cahokia
cahokia.summary: The largest Native American city north of Mexico, inhabited from about 1050 to 1350 CE near present-day St. Louis, with around 120 earthworks and a peak population of up to 20,000.

spiro-mounds.name: Spiro Mounds
spiro-mounds.summary: A major archaeological site in eastern Oklahoma that served as a religious and political center of the Caddoan Mississippian culture between the 9th and 15th centuries.

kiva.name: Kiva
kiva.summary: An underground room used by Puebloans for spiritual ceremonies, worship and political meetings, evolved from earlier pit-houses and found among ancient ruins across the Southwestern United States.

wickliffe-mounds.name: Wickliffe Mounds
wickliffe-mounds.summary: A prehistoric Mississippian culture archaeological site in Kentucky near the confluence of the Ohio and Mississippi rivers, now a museum and historic site.

mississippian-period-archaeology.name: Mississippian period
mississippian-period-archaeology.summary: An archaeological era (roughly 10th–16th centuries) in the Southern and Eastern United States marked by maize farming, population centers, and large platform mounds.

saga-of-the-greenlanders.name: Saga of the Greenlanders
saga-of-the-greenlanders.summary: One of two main Icelandic sources on the Norse colonization of North America, describing events around 1000 CE, including six expeditions from Greenland led by figures such as Leif Erikson and Freydís Eiríksdóttir.

saga-of-erik-the-red.name: Saga of Erik the Red
saga-of-erik-the-red.summary: A 13th-century Icelandic saga on Norse exploration of North America, mainly chronicling the expedition of Thorfinn Karlsefni and Gudrid, including Erik the Red's exile to Greenland and Leif Erikson's discovery of Vinland.

haudenosaunee.name: Haudenosaunee
haudenosaunee.summary: A confederacy of Iroquoian-speaking peoples in northeast North America, originally five (later six) nations united under the Great Law of Peace, called the Iroquois by Europeans.

great-peacemaker.name: Great Peacemaker
great-peacemaker.summary: Traditional co-founder, with Jigonhsasee and Hiawatha, of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy, a union of six Iroquoian-speaking nations across parts of New York, Pennsylvania, Ontario and Quebec.

hiawatha.name: Hiawatha
hiawatha.summary: Likely 12th- or 15th-century leader of the Onondaga or Mohawk people who cofounded the Haudenosaunee Confederacy in the eastern Great Lakes region.

wampum.name: Wampum
wampum.summary: Traditional shell beads made by Indigenous peoples of Northeastern North America, used before European contact for storytelling, ceremonial gifts and recording treaties, and later adopted by Europeans as a form of currency.

flateyjarb-k.name: Flateyjarbók
flateyjarb-k.summary: A medieval Icelandic manuscript, the 'Book of Flatey', commissioned by lawspeaker Jón Hákonarson and produced by the priest-scribes Jón Þórðarson and Magnús Þórhallsson.

bjarni-herj-lfsson.name: Bjarni Herjólfsson
bjarni-herj-lfsson.summary: An Icelandic explorer believed to be the first known European to sight the mainland of the Americas, in 986.

leif-erikson.name: Leif Erikson
leif-erikson.summary: A Norse explorer (c. 970s–c. 1018/1025) thought to be the first European to reach continental America, establishing a settlement at Vinland about five centuries before Columbus.

freyd-s-eir-ksd-ttir.name: Freydís Eiríksdóttir
freyd-s-eir-ksd-ttir.summary: An Icelandic woman, daughter of Erik the Red, said to have taken part in Norse exploration of North America as an early colonist of Vinland.

vinland.name: Vinland
vinland.summary: Area of coastal North America explored by Vikings, where Leif Erikson landed around AD 1000, long before Columbus; Norse building remains confirming it were found at L'Anse aux Meadows, Newfoundland, in 1960.

thorfinn-karlsefni.name: Thorfinn Karlsefni
thorfinn-karlsefni.summary: An Icelandic explorer who around 1010 followed Leif Eriksson's route to Vinland, attempting with his wife Gudrid to found a permanent settlement there.

gudrid-thorbjarnard-ttir.name: Gudrid Thorbjarnardóttir
gudrid-thorbjarnard-ttir.summary: An Icelandic explorer (c. 980–1019) who sailed to Vinland with her husband Thorfinn Karlsefni; their son Snorri was the first European known born in the Americas outside Greenland.

sagas-of-icelanders.name: Sagas of Icelanders
sagas-of-icelanders.summary: A group of Old Icelandic prose narratives, mostly based on real events in Iceland's ninth to eleventh centuries and recorded in the 13th and 14th centuries; the best-known works of Icelandic literature.

tadodaho.name: Tadodaho
tadodaho.summary: A legendary Onondaga leader feared as a sorcerer, persuaded by the Great Peacemaker and Hiawatha to help found the Haudenosaunee Confederacy as its firekeeper.

onondaga-people.name: Onondaga
onondaga-people.summary: One of the five original nations of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy, historically based south of Lake Ontario in present-day New York; known as 'Keepers of the Fire' for hosting the confederacy's council.

great-law-of-peace.name: Great Law of Peace
great-law-of-peace.summary: The oral constitution of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy, established around 1100 CE among five Iroquoian nations, recorded on wampum belts and divided into 117 articles.

hauksb-k.name: Hauksbók
hauksb-k.summary: A 14th-century Icelandic manuscript compiled by Haukr Erlendsson, preserving the earliest surviving copies of several sagas, including the Saga of Erik the Red.

sk-lholtsb-k.name: Skálholtsbók
sk-lholtsb-k.summary: A 15th-century Icelandic manuscript of sagas, including a copy of the Saga of Erik the Red, likely written by Ólafur Loftsson.

haukr-erlendsson.name: Haukr Erlendsson
haukr-erlendsson.summary: Icelandic lawspeaker who died in 1334, later also a lawspeaker and knight in Norway, best known for compiling Icelandic sagas into the manuscript named after him.

markland.name: Markland
markland.summary: One of three lands on North America's Atlantic coast, south of Helluland and north of Vinland, discovered by Leif Eriksson around 1000 AD; likely visited later for timber though never settled.

skr-ling.name: Skræling
skr-ling.summary: The Old Norse name Norse Greenlanders used for peoples they encountered in North America, including the Thule people and, in Vinland, Indigenous inhabitants.

great-ireland.name: Hvítramannaland
great-ireland.summary: A legendary land the Norse said lay near Vinland, also called White Men's Land, described in sagas as home to people in white garments; scholars disagree whether it was myth or a real North American location.

orbj-rg-l-tilv-lva.name: Þorbjörg lítilvölva
orbj-rg-l-tilv-lva.summary: A renowned seeress, or völva, in Norse colonial Greenland during the late Viking Age, featured in the Saga of Erik the Red.

old-norse-religion.name: Old Norse religion
old-norse-religion.summary: The polytheistic religion of the North Germanic peoples before Christianity, featuring gods such as Odin and Thor and a mythology centered on the world tree Yggdrasil.

tree-of-peace.name: Tree of Peace
tree-of-peace.summary: An eastern white pine symbolizing the Haudenosaunee Confederacy and its oral constitution, rooted in the legendary peacemaker Dekanawida who united the Five Nations.

patricia-sutherland.name: Patricia Sutherland
patricia-sutherland.summary: A Canadian Arctic archaeologist whose research on Baffin Island suggests a Norse presence and trade with the Dorset people centuries before Norse Greenland settlement, a controversial theory.

mesa-verde-national-park.name: Mesa Verde
mesa-verde-national-park.summary: A US national park in Colorado preserving thousands of Ancestral Puebloan sites, including the Cliff Palace, and seasonally inhabited by Paleo-Indians from around 7500 BCE.

hohokam.name: Hohokam
hohokam.summary: A culture of the North American Southwest, in south-central Arizona and Sonora, Mexico, that existed from about 300 to 1500 CE and is known for large-scale irrigation canals.

dean-snow.name: Dean Snow
dean-snow.summary: American archaeologist and ethnohistorian, professor emeritus at Pennsylvania State University, who researched Iroquois nations and other indigenous cultures in Mexico, Spain and France; in 1977 he advised the Justice Department on Maine Indian land claims.

woodland-period.name: Woodland period
woodland-period.summary: An archaeological period of pre-Columbian eastern North America lasting from about 1000 BCE to European contact, marked by continuous development and the spread of pottery.

monks-mound.name: Monks Mound
monks-mound.summary: The largest prehistoric earthwork in the Americas, built from about 900 to 955 CE at Cahokia in Illinois, with a base roughly as large as the Great Pyramid of Giza.

jigonhsasee.name: Jigonhsasee
jigonhsasee.summary: An Iroquoian woman honored as co-founder, with the Great Peacemaker and Hiawatha, of the Haudenosaunee Confederacy, known as the Mother of Nations and Head Clan Mother.

thule-people.name: Thule people
thule-people.summary: The precursors of modern Inuit and Yupik peoples, who developed in coastal Alaska by 1000 CE, spread across the Arctic, and replaced the earlier Dorset culture by the 15th century.

dorset-culture.name: Dorset culture
dorset-culture.summary: A Paleo-Eskimo culture in the North American Arctic, lasting from about 500 BCE until it died out by 1000–1500 CE, before the Thule (proto-Inuit) arrived. Inuit legends recall its people as the Tuniit.

gar-ar-greenland.name: Garðar
gar-ar-greenland.summary: The seat of the bishop in Norse Greenland, and the first Catholic diocese established anywhere in the Americas.

yupik-peoples.name: Yup'ik
yupik-peoples.summary: Indigenous peoples of western and southcentral Alaska and the Russian Far East, closely related to the Inuit and Iñupiat.

iroquoian-peoples.name: Iroquoian peoples
iroquoian-peoples.summary: An ethnolinguistic group of Native American peoples in eastern North America, including the Haudenosaunee and Cherokee, whose distinctive culture had developed by about 1000 AD.

western-settlement.name: Western Settlement
western-settlement.summary: A Norse farming community in medieval Greenland founded around 985, smaller than its companion Eastern Settlement and found abandoned when last visited in the 14th century.
